title: Subpolynomial detection of two-connected patterns
formal: Does there exist a fixed finite simple 2-vertex-connected graph H, with at least three vertices, for which exact H-subgraph detection in the randomized CONGEST model can be solved in \(n^{o(1)}\) rounds on every n-vertex network? The pattern is fixed independently of n. Detection means that, with probability at least \(2/3\), every node outputs NO when the network contains no copy of H, and at least one node outputs YES when it does contain a copy.
context:
The source contrasts constant-round detection of every fixed tree with polynomial lower bounds for cycles of length at least four and other pattern classes. Its reductions transfer hardness from a 2-connected block to larger connected patterns, motivating the focus on 2-connected graphs.

Standard distributed detection allows any one node to signal existence. Requiring every node to learn that a distant copy exists would add an unrelated distance cost and would change the constant-round comparison with trees.

The revised survey keeps the complexity of triangle detection open. Assadi and Sundaresan give an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) lower bound, while the known upper bounds are polynomial in n. This is significant progress, but a logarithmic lower bound does not exclude \(n^{o(1)}\) detection.

Listing requires every copy to be reported; detection needs only one existence signal. The known polynomial lower bounds for triangle listing therefore do not establish a polynomial detection lower bound or settle the all-pattern question.
why: Asks whether any cyclic pattern can be detected almost as quickly as trees under per-edge communication limits. A resolution would clarify a broad boundary in distributed graph algorithms, and its negative direction includes the difficult triangle-detection barrier.
status_note: Read the original question and surrounding graph-class interpretation; checked the 2025 survey’s standard output convention and the newer triangle lower bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no subpolynomial algorithm for an eligible pattern or a resolution excluding all of them. The reported logarithmic triangle bound does not prove polynomial hardness. Proofs were not independently audited.

progress.text: The OPODIS source proves hardness transfers for pattern classes and asks whether any fixed 2-connected pattern admits subpolynomial detection.
Assadi and Sundaresan report the first general multi-round lower bound for triangle detection, \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\); the checked revision is from 13 August 2025.
The survey’s fifth revision incorporates this bound and retains the open triangle-detection question.

The primary source’s Definition 1 reverses the H-free/containing cases for all-accept versus some-reject, and Definition 2 says deleting k vertices where standard k-connectivity concerns fewer than k. Literal use would conflict with its tree comparison and cycle examples. These wording problems are recorded rather than copied into the card. The intended 2-vertex-connected and ordinary detection conventions are explicit; no unanimous global decision or listing task was substituted.

importance.reason: A structural existence question about the distributed complexity of cyclic graph patterns, encompassing the unresolved communication barrier for triangles. Existing score retained.

sentences: The question asks whether any fixed 2-vertex-connected graph can be detected in subpolynomial CONGEST rounds.
Nodes can exchange only logarithmically many bits per edge per round.
Exact detection requires one node to signal an existing copy and all nodes to stay negative when none exists.
Trees have constant-round algorithms, while many cyclic patterns have polynomial lower bounds.
The newer logarithmic lower bound for triangles leaves the requested subpolynomial-versus-harder boundary unresolved.

references.title: Lower Bounds for Subgraph Detection in the CONGEST Model
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 15; PDF page 15

definitions:
The pattern H is an undirected finite simple graph. It is 2-vertex-connected if it has at least three vertices, is connected and remains connected after deleting any single vertex and its incident edges. This excludes an isolated edge and includes triangles and longer cycles. The network G is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph on n vertices. A copy of H is an injective map \(\varphi :V(H)\to V(G)\) such that every edge uv of H maps to an edge \(\varphi (u)\varphi (v)\) of G. Extra edges among the images are allowed: the task is not induced-subgraph detection, homomorphism, minor containment or property testing with a distance promise.

There is one processor at each vertex. Each knows n, H, its own distinct identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors; identifiers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, and the guarantee must hold for every valid assignment of identifiers. Local edges have identifiable ports. In each synchronous round a node may send a different message of at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to each neighbor, for a fixed constant B independent of n. Messages are received before the next round, and later messages may depend on everything received so far. No communication is allowed across nonedges. Local computation and memory are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. This is ordinary CONGEST, with distinct messages permitted on distinct edges, not broadcast CONGEST or the congested clique.

The algorithm is a uniform distributed procedure fixed with H; it may use independent private random bits at the nodes. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. It halts within a worst-case bound \(T_{H}(n)\) on every network, identifier assignment and random tape. The success event concerns the joint vector of all node outputs, with probability over all random bits. In an H-free network all outputs must be NO simultaneously; in a network containing H one YES anywhere suffices. There is no requirement that the detecting node belong to a copy, identify its vertices, list all copies, or notify distant nodes. Disconnected networks are permitted and the same global output convention applies.

The required bound \(n^{o(1)}\) means that one such algorithm exists with \(\log (\max \{2,T_{H}(n)\})/\log  n\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty\). Equivalently, for every fixed \(\delta >0\) its worst-case round bound is at most \(n^{\delta}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants and the threshold length may depend on H and \(\delta\). A family of different algorithms, one for each \(\delta\), is not silently identified with that single-algorithm claim. A bound \(n^{\alpha _{H}}\) with a fixed positive \(\alpha _{H}\), even a very small one, is not subpolynomial. The size of H is a constant, not another growing complexity parameter.

The source also asks whether every 2-connected pattern instead requires a polynomial number of rounds. A theorem giving each fixed H a lower bound \(\Omega (n^{\delta _{H}})\) for some \(\delta _{H}>0\) would refute the existence question, but this stronger growth dichotomy is not assumed to be its logical negation. A negative answer here only needs to exclude the stated \(n^{o(1)}\) algorithms for every eligible H.
answer_criterion: A positive answer provides one fixed eligible H and proves a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm with the stated global success probability and \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case rounds. A negative answer rules out such an algorithm for every fixed eligible H. A lower bound for only one pattern, or a fast algorithm for induced copies, promised-far graphs, listing in another model or a pattern that grows with n, does not settle this existence question.
